Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-12
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Recruiter), Marcos Rivera (Hiring Manager), Sofia Liu (Interviewer), Maya Patel (Candidate)

[00:00] Jordan Ellis: hey everyone, thanks for joining, Maya thanks for taking the screen today, we're doing a 40-ish minute tech-focused call, quick intros then some systems questions, then time for you to ask questions.
[00:12] Maya Patel: yeah, thanks for having me, excited to chat.
[00:18] Marcos Rivera: hi Maya, I'm Marcos, I run inference infra here, curious about the projects you listed on your resume especially the Triton migration you mentioned.
[00:28] Maya Patel: cool. so at my last role I led a migration from a legacy REST GPU pool to NVIDIA Triton, and that included writing custom backends for a few model families and integrating dynamic batching. We moved from a bunch of ad-hoc servers to a consolidated Triton cluster fronted by a routing layer. I worked on performance profiles and kernel selection heuristics, plus a KV prefix cache for short-lived conversations.
[00:45] Sofia Liu: when you say KV prefix cache, do you mean an in-process cache on the serving nodes or a shared cache?
[00:52] Maya Patel: it was hybrid, actually. short prefixes were stored in LRU in-process to avoid RPC for tiny sequences, and then we backed that with a shared Redis layer for larger contexts. We also did optimistic cache warming when a conversation looked hot.
[01:04] Marcos Rivera: any quantization experience? we do a lot of 8-bit and mixed precision tradeoffs.
[01:09] Maya Patel: yes, I ran a small study comparing 8-bit post-training quantization vs 4-bit experimental quant on a set of customer workloads. 8-bit gave .3 to .8% quality delta in most tasks and cut memory by about 40%. I also helped tune kernel launches to make 8-bit matrix ops efficient on Ampere.
[01:24] [background noise/interruption] Speaker 4: sorry, little echo.
[01:30] Sofia Liu: can you walk us through a time you debugged a production OOM or perf regression? what was the tooling and root cause?
[01:37] Maya Patel: sure. we had a regression after a model update where p99 latency spiked and GPUs OOM'd intermittently. I pulled traces from our request logs, correlated with GPU memory snapshots and NVidia SMI dumps. We found a change in the tokenizer that increased average sequence length by ~30%, which blew up KV cache and per-request allocation. Quick mitigation was to bump eviction thresholds and enable prefix truncation, then we rolled a small rollback for the tokenizer. For longer-term I worked with infra to add sequence-length-based routing: short sequences to a high-throughput pool, long sequences to a high-memory pool.
[02:15] Jordan Ellis: nice, that matches problems we see. what's your experience with continuous batching approaches?
[02:21] Maya Patel: implemented a continuous batching layer that aggregated requests up to timeout or token budget, similar to radix-style. We had to tune per-model timeouts to hit latency SLOs; we also used adaptive batching — lower batch sizes for latency-critical routes. The tricky bit was memory fragmentation on CUDA and ensuring KV cache semantics didn't conflict with batching.
[02:41] Marcos Rivera: how comfortable are you with low-level kernel selection and CUDA tuning, like launch bounds, shared mem usage?
[02:48] Maya Patel: comfortable. I wrote a few CUDA kernels for attention variants in a research project and profiled them with Nsight and nvprof. I have experience adjusting launch parameters, memory coalescing, and avoiding bank conflicts. I haven't authored a full fused transformer kernel in prod, but I can navigate and optimize kernels and trade off precision to improve throughput.
[03:07] Sofia Liu: we sometimes need to implement graceful degradation and fallbacks, e.g., drop to smaller model when capacity constrained. talk about a design for such routing.
[03:16] Maya Patel: you need multi-dimension routing — route by latency SLO, cost budget, and data residency. Have a policy manager that maps incoming request metadata to a route: prefer full-precision model on dedicated pool, otherwise route to quantized model or cached response, and finally a cheap completion model. Metrics and tracing to ensure we don't silently lower quality. Also can use priority queues for bursty traffic.
[03:38] [crosstalk] Marcos Rivera: ...and you'd expose that via..
[03:40] Maya Patel: an API with route hints and request-level priority.
[03:44] Jordan Ellis: switching gears — behavioral: tell us about a time you influenced a skeptical team or led a rollout.
[03:51] Maya Patel: when we moved to Triton there was pushback over control loss. I built a transparent staging pipeline, plus a few dashboards that showed model-level latency/cost differences and a canary traffic pattern. I ran A/B tests, so engineers could see parity. Documentation and a try-it playground helped.
[04:10] Sofia Liu: quick whiteboard question — say you're given intermittent 5–10% token-level hallucination increases after a quantization change. how do you triage?
[04:20] Maya Patel: start with diffing model outputs on a curated eval set; measure hallucination with heuristics and embeddings-based similarity. Rollback if it's clearly worse. If marginal, try fine-tuning quantization parameters, reduce quant granularity, or use selective higher-precision layers for critical heads. Also check tokenization differences and any preprocessing drift.
[04:45] Marcos Rivera: what's your interviewing availability for onsite? and expectation on notice period?
[04:50] Maya Patel: I'm available next week afternoons for deep dives; 2-week notice to current employer is what I'd expect.
[04:58] Jordan Ellis: great. any questions for us?
[05:02] Maya Patel: yeah, curious about the largest scale workload you run for latency-sensitive inference and what SLOs you target?
[05:08] Marcos Rivera: our hosted API routes aim for p50 < 40ms token and p95 depends on model size — up to 800ms for large 32k context models; dedicated customers sometimes have stricter constraints. There's also the routing layer complexities.
[05:25] Maya Patel: cool, that aligns with my experience.
[05:29] Sofia Liu: final quick check — what languages/tools do you prefer for infra code?
[05:33] Maya Patel: Python for orchestration, Go for critical path services, some Rust experiments. CUDA C++ for kernels and benchmark harnesses.
[05:41] [awkward silence] Jordan Ellis: okay thanks, we'll wrap. Next steps: Jordan will send the take-home, Sofia will prepare the onsite plan. Marcos will confirm hiring band. Expect feedback in 3-4 business days.
[05:56] Maya Patel: thanks everyone, appreciate it.
